title: AP World History: Modern
summary: Compare states, exchange networks, empires and global change from about 1200 onward.
frameworkNote: 2026–27 structure checked against College Board on 15 October 2026: 9 units. Original VertexED focused lessons and self-check questions sample each unit; they do not replace the full course framework, required materials or teacher review. Nine units cover the current modern-world framework from about 1200. May 2027 short-answer and long-essay exam changes do not alter course content; no exercise here is an official exam item.

modules.title: 1200–1450: Comparing states and societies
modules.focus: Compare a shared governing problem across different settings.
explanation: Around 1200–1450, states and communities across the world organised authority through varied institutions, beliefs and social relationships. Compare specific cases on a common dimension, such as recruitment of officials or the relationship between rulers and religion.

In Song China, examinations helped connect elite education with government service, while other states relied on different combinations of hereditary status, military power and religious authority. Similarity in one function does not make institutions identical or imply that all residents experienced power equally.

workedExample.prompt: Compare two rulers who use religious ideas to support authority but govern different institutions.
steps: Identify the shared function: presenting rule as legitimate.
Explain the different institutions and contexts through which that claim operates.

misconception.claim: All societies developed through the same sequence towards one model.
misconception.correction: Historical paths varied and interacted; comparison should not assume a universal ranking.

questions.prompt: Why use the same comparison criterion for two states?
questions.hint: Consider what makes a comparison meaningful.
questions.answer: A shared criterion allows a clear similarity or difference rather than two disconnected descriptions.

questions.prompt: What limitation should accompany a claim about examination-based recruitment?
questions.answer: Educational resources and social position affected who could prepare and succeed, so the system did not create equal access for everyone.

questions.prompt: Why should two rulers' religious claims not be taken as proof of identical institutions?
questions.answer: Religion can support authority in both cases. Taxation and recruitment may still differ. The comparison should examine those institutions directly.
checkpoints: Religion can support authority in both cases.
Taxation and recruitment may still differ.
The comparison should examine those institutions directly.

questions.prompt: A source praises a state's examinations as merit-based. What additional evidence would test social access?
questions.answer: Records of candidates' backgrounds would help. Costs and availability of education matter. These show whether formal competition translated into broad opportunity.
checkpoints: Records of candidates' backgrounds would help.
Costs and availability of education matter.
These show whether formal competition translated into broad opportunity.

notes.title: 1200–1450: Comparing states and societies in depth
paragraphs: Comparison needs a common question before differences become meaningful. Song China's examination system connected classical learning to official recruitment, but preparation depended heavily on resources and access. Other states organised service through hereditary, military or religious networks. None of these descriptions means that one institution governed every aspect of society. Compare how officials were selected, how revenue was gathered and how rulers justified authority. A formal route into government may widen opportunity relative to inheritance while remaining unequal in practice. Institutional design and the social distribution of access therefore need separate evidence.

workedExamples.prompt: Compare a hypothetical examination-based recruitment system with hereditary officeholding.
steps: An examination sets a formal knowledge requirement, while hereditary office ties eligibility to family position.
Costly preparation can still favour wealthy families in the examination system.
workedExamples.conclusion: The comparison identifies a real institutional difference without treating the examination route as universal equality.

flashcards.back: A shared criterion and explained similarities or differences.
Classical education and official recruitment.

flashcards.front: Does formal eligibility guarantee equal access?
flashcards.back: No.
Office transmitted or restricted through family descent.

modules.title: 1200–1450: Exchange networks and consequences
modules.focus: Connect trade infrastructure to cultural and biological change.
explanation: Silk Road, Indian Ocean and trans-Saharan networks connected regions through different transport systems and environments. Commercial practices, political protection and technologies could lower risks and expand exchange. Compare mechanisms rather than merely listing traded goods.

Merchants, travellers and religious communities also moved ideas, practices and pathogens. The same connections that supported prosperity could transmit disease. Cultural change involved adaptation and local choices rather than simple replacement of one culture by another.

workedExample.prompt: Explain how caravanserais could support overland exchange.
steps: Rest stops offered shelter, supplies and opportunities to exchange information.
Reduced risks and costs made longer commercial journeys more feasible.

misconception.claim: Trade routes carried only physical goods.
misconception.correction: People also carried knowledge, beliefs, technologies and diseases.

questions.prompt: Why did monsoon knowledge matter to Indian Ocean trade?
questions.answer: It helped sailors plan departures and return journeys, making maritime travel more reliable.

questions.prompt: How could expanded trade create both benefit and harm?
questions.answer: It could increase commercial exchange and cultural contact while also enabling pathogens to spread between connected populations.

questions.prompt: Why can the same network carry both commercial benefits and disease risks?
hints: Do not treat outcomes as mutually exclusive.
questions.answer: Connections bring traders and communities into contact. Those contacts can circulate pathogens as well as goods. Prosperity and disease exposure can therefore increase together.
checkpoints: Connections bring traders and communities into contact.
Those contacts can circulate pathogens as well as goods.
Prosperity and disease exposure can therefore increase together.

questions.prompt: A foreign religious practice gains local imagery after arrival. What does this show about diffusion?
hints: Avoid calling change a failed copy.
questions.answer: The practice moved through a network. Local participants reshaped its expression. Diffusion can involve selective adaptation rather than complete cultural replacement.
checkpoints: The practice moved through a network.
Diffusion can involve selective adaptation rather than complete cultural replacement.

notes.title: 1200–1450: Exchange networks and consequences in depth
paragraphs: Exchange networks depended on physical routes and institutions that reduced risk. Caravanserais could provide stopping places for overland travellers, while credit and commercial partnerships could reduce the need to carry all value as goods or coin. Indian Ocean sailing also depended on seasonal winds and local maritime knowledge. Goods, beliefs and pathogens travelled through connected populations, though not with identical routes or effects. A network's growth can support prosperity and vulnerability at the same time. Local communities adapted imported practices, so diffusion should not be described as one-way replacement without evidence.

workedExamples.prompt: Explain a hypothetical merchant's choice to use a route with regular caravanserais despite a slightly longer distance.
steps: Stopping places can improve access to shelter, supplies and information.
Reduced uncertainty may outweigh some additional travel time.
workedExamples.conclusion: Trade routes reflect risk and institutions as well as the shortest geographical path.

flashcards.back: Stopping places supporting overland travel and exchange.
It can facilitate transactions without carrying all payment physically.

flashcards.front: What shaped Indian Ocean sailing seasons?
flashcards.back: Monsoon wind patterns.
No; adaptation is common.

diagrams.title: Trade beyond distance
diagrams.description: Institutions change the practical cost of movement.

nodes.detail: Travellers face supply and information risks.

nodes.label: Caravanserai network
nodes.detail: Stopping places reduce some uncertainty.

nodes.detail: More journeys may become viable.

modules.title: 1450–1750: Governing large land empires
modules.focus: Explain how rulers combined coercion, administration and legitimacy.
explanation: Large land empires used military capacity, taxation and administrative arrangements to govern diverse populations. Gunpowder weapons contributed to expansion in some settings, but resources, organisation and alliances also mattered. Technology alone does not explain imperial success.

Rulers used religious ideas, monumental architecture and patronage to legitimise authority. Policies towards diversity varied across time and place. Compare Ottoman, Safavid and Mughal institutions through specific evidence rather than treating them as interchangeable.

workedExample.prompt: Explain why building a monumental capital might strengthen imperial rule.
steps: Its scale and design could display wealth, order and authority.
It could also concentrate administration and ritual, though maintaining it required resources.

misconception.correction: Organisation, finance, strategy and opponents’ responses also shaped outcomes.

questions.prompt: Why might an empire use local elites in administration?
questions.answer: Local elites could supply knowledge and legitimacy that helped collect taxes and govern, while creating dependence or rivalry.

questions.prompt: How can religious patronage function politically?
questions.answer: Support for institutions or rituals can associate the ruler with valued traditions and strengthen claims to legitimacy.

questions.prompt: Why is 'gunpowder caused imperial success' an incomplete explanation?
questions.hint: Ask how weapons are supplied and used.
hints: Ask how weapons are supplied and used.
questions.answer: Weapons require financing and logistics. Organisation and alliances affect their use. Technology is one factor within a wider political system.
checkpoints: Organisation and alliances affect their use.
Technology is one factor within a wider political system.

questions.prompt: A monumental palace proclaims unity while provinces retain different laws. Is this necessarily contradictory evidence?
questions.answer: The palace communicates a central claim of authority. Administrative diversity may remain practical. A unified image need not imply identical provincial institutions.
checkpoints: The palace communicates a central claim of authority.
A unified image need not imply identical provincial institutions.

notes.title: 1450–1750: Governing large land empires in depth
paragraphs: Large land empires needed ways to collect revenue and manage relationships across diverse territories. Military technology could assist expansion, but armies also required finance, supplies and loyal personnel. Ottoman, Safavid and Mughal rulers used different administrative and religious arrangements, and those arrangements changed over time. Monumental building and court patronage could display legitimacy while provincial negotiation made rule workable. Distinguish a ruler's ideological claim from the everyday mechanisms of administration. Comparing diversity policies requires a particular reign or context rather than treating an empire's several centuries as one unchanging policy.

workedExamples.prompt: Analyse a hypothetical empire granting provincial officials revenue rights in return for service.
steps: The arrangement connects local collection to the centre's need for personnel and resources.
It can extend reach while giving officials interests and bargaining power.
workedExamples.conclusion: Delegation supports empire but can also create limits on central control.

flashcards.front: What does imperial administration require besides weapons?
flashcards.back: Revenue, supplies, personnel and coordination.
A claim or belief that authority is rightful.

flashcards.front: Why specify a reign when comparing policies?
flashcards.back: Policies change over time.

flashcards.front: Can delegation both strengthen and limit a ruler?
flashcards.back: Yes.

diagrams.description: Expansion depends on an administrative relationship.

nodes.detail: Local officials collect and transfer resources.

nodes.detail: Cooperation extends reach but creates dependence.

modules.title: 1450–1750: Maritime empires and coerced labour
modules.focus: Trace connections between oceanic expansion and social change.
explanation: Maritime expansion connected the Americas, Africa, Europe and Asia through new routes and unequal relationships. States and trading companies sought revenue, strategic positions and commercial advantages. Existing Asian and African networks continued to shape the terms of exchange.

Colonisation, plantation production and the Atlantic slave trade depended on coercion and produced resistance. The movement of crops, animals and pathogens changed environments and populations, with particularly devastating disease effects among Indigenous American communities.

workedExample.prompt: Explain a link between plantation sugar demand and the expansion of Atlantic slavery.
steps: Profitable sugar cultivation required intensive labour under plantation conditions.
Enslavers expanded forced transportation and coercive labour to pursue that demand, while enslaved people resisted.

misconception.claim: Oceanic expansion replaced all older trading networks.
misconception.correction: New routes interacted with and sometimes redirected networks that already existed.

questions.prompt: Why distinguish voluntary migration from forced transportation?
questions.answer: The conditions, coercion and consequences differ fundamentally; grouping them together can conceal violence and lack of consent.

questions.prompt: How could an introduced crop change life far from its origin?
questions.answer: A suitable crop could alter diets, farming choices and population support, depending on local conditions and adoption.

questions.prompt: Why should the spread of an American crop into Eurasia not be described as having one identical effect everywhere?
questions.answer: Growing conditions differ. Food systems and labour arrangements shape use. Population and dietary effects therefore require regional evidence.
checkpoints: Food systems and labour arrangements shape use.
Population and dietary effects therefore require regional evidence.

questions.prompt: A company charter authorises forts and armed forces. What does it reveal about commerce and empire?
questions.hint: Identify powers beyond buying and selling.
hints: Identify powers beyond buying and selling.
questions.answer: The company has coercive capacities. Those powers can secure routes or impose terms. Commercial activity is intertwined with political authority.
checkpoints: Those powers can secure routes or impose terms.
Commercial activity is intertwined with political authority.

notes.title: 1450–1750: Maritime empires and coerced labour in depth
paragraphs: Maritime empires combined ocean routes with forts, colonies and commercial institutions, but their control was uneven. Trading companies could exercise coercive powers as well as pursue profit. Plantation demand linked land seizure and enslaved labour to distant consumption, while enslaved people and Indigenous communities resisted these systems. The Columbian Exchange changed environments through crops, animals and pathogens. Biological transfer was not equal in its consequences, and disease interacted with violence and displacement. An explanation should identify who moved what, under which constraints, and who bore the costs of the resulting connections.

workedExamples.prompt: Trace a hypothetical sugar plantation's link to distant buyers.
steps: Demand gives merchants and planters an incentive to expand production.
Expansion relies in this case on coerced labour and land control, not simply a neutral market transaction.
workedExamples.conclusion: The commodity chain joins consumer demand to institutions of violence and to resistance by those subjected to them.

flashcards.back: Large-scale agricultural production often oriented towards distant markets.

flashcards.front: Were maritime companies purely nonpolitical traders?
flashcards.back: No; some exercised coercive and governing powers.

flashcards.front: What did the Columbian Exchange move?
flashcards.back: Organisms and diseases between previously separated regions.
No.

modules.title: 1750–1900: Revolutions and industrial change
modules.focus: Connect ideas with material conditions and political action.
explanation: Political revolutions drew on changing ideas about sovereignty and rights while responding to local inequalities and conflicts. Enlightenment arguments did not produce identical outcomes everywhere. The Haitian Revolution, for example, challenged slavery and colonial rule through enslaved people’s struggle.

Industrialisation changed production using energy, machinery, capital and labour organisation. Its spread depended on resources and institutions as well as technology. Explain how political and economic changes interacted while preserving differences in timing, actors and consequences.

workedExample.prompt: Compare claims about liberty in a revolution led by colonial elites with those of enslaved revolutionaries.
steps: Both might challenge an existing authority using rights language.
The social meaning and intended reach of freedom could differ sharply, especially concerning slavery.

misconception.claim: A shared revolutionary vocabulary means identical goals.
misconception.correction: Different groups used similar language to demand different changes.

questions.prompt: Why include coal, investment and labour when explaining industrialisation?
questions.answer: Machines required energy, financing and workers to become a sustained system of production.

questions.prompt: How can an industrial innovation affect political demands?
questions.answer: Factory growth can concentrate workers and expose shared conditions, encouraging organisation and demands for regulation or representation.

questions.prompt: Why should the Haitian Revolution not be explained merely as European ideas reaching passive recipients?
questions.answer: Enslaved people organised and fought for freedom. They interpreted and transformed rights claims through their circumstances. Their agency is central to the revolution's course.
checkpoints: Enslaved people organised and fought for freedom.
They interpreted and transformed rights claims through their circumstances.
Their agency is central to the revolution's course.

questions.prompt: A region possesses coal but industrialises slowly. What does this show?
questions.answer: Coal alone is insufficient. Capital, transport, labour and institutions affect adoption. Industrialisation requires a combination of conditions rather than one resource.
checkpoints: Capital, transport, labour and institutions affect adoption.
Industrialisation requires a combination of conditions rather than one resource.

notes.title: 1750–1900: Revolutions and industrial change in depth
paragraphs: Revolutionary rights language travelled across the Atlantic but acquired different meanings through local struggles. In Haiti, enslaved people challenged slavery and colonial domination, making freedom from ownership central rather than treating independence as only a change of rulers. Industrialisation likewise involved more than invention: energy, investment, markets and labour arrangements affected adoption. Political and economic changes could interact without following one universal sequence. Compare the actors, rights claimed and material conditions in each case. A declaration's language is evidence of a principle, while institutions and lived conditions show how far it was implemented.

workedExamples.prompt: Compare a hypothetical colonial elite's demand for self-government with enslaved workers' demand for emancipation.
steps: The first challenges external political authority but may leave labour hierarchy intact.
The second challenges the legal ownership of persons.
workedExamples.conclusion: Both invoke freedom, but their institutional targets and beneficiaries can differ substantially.

flashcards.front: What made emancipation distinct from colonial self-government?
flashcards.back: It ended a form of ownership and coercive legal status.

flashcards.front: What was central to the Haitian Revolution?
flashcards.back: Struggle against slavery and colonial rule.
No.
Principles and implementation can diverge.

diagrams.description: A shared word can identify different political targets.

nodes.detail: Challenges rule from a colonial centre.

nodes.label: Emancipation claim

modules.title: 1750–1900: Empire, migration and unequal economies
modules.focus: Explain how industrial power altered global relationships.
explanation: Industrial states expanded imperial influence through military force, finance and political agreements. Economic motives interacted with nationalism, strategic competition and racial ideologies. Colonised societies resisted, negotiated and adapted, so their agency belongs in the explanation.

Global migration included indentured labour, coerced movement and voluntary migration under unequal constraints. Export-oriented economies could become dependent on particular commodities and external markets. Benefits and costs differed among officials, merchants, workers and communities.

workedExample.prompt: Explain how an export railway could serve imperial economic priorities.
steps: A route from a producing region to a port could move raw materials efficiently.
Its design might prioritise export extraction over connections among local communities.

misconception.claim: Every railway automatically served local development equally.
misconception.correction: Route design, ownership and access shaped who benefited.

questions.prompt: Why might dependence on one export crop create vulnerability?
questions.answer: A price fall or crop failure could sharply reduce income because alternative sources were limited.

questions.prompt: How can migrant letters improve a study based on recruitment contracts?
questions.answer: Letters may reveal actual conditions, family strategies and unmet promises that the contract’s official language omits.

questions.prompt: Why can a fall in a global commodity price affect a distant producing region?
questions.answer: Export revenue falls when the price drops, other things equal. Employers and public revenue may be affected. Workers and households can bear costs despite being far from the buyers.
checkpoints: Export revenue falls when the price drops, other things equal.
Employers and public revenue may be affected.
Workers and households can bear costs despite being far from the buyers.

questions.prompt: How would you compare two migrant contracts without assuming both were freely chosen?
questions.answer: Compare promised and actual conditions. Examine debt, penalties and freedom to leave. Assess the choices available before and during the contract.
checkpoints: Examine debt, penalties and freedom to leave.
Assess the choices available before and during the contract.

notes.title: 1750–1900: Empire, migration and unequal economies in depth
paragraphs: Imperial infrastructure could connect an export zone efficiently to a port while doing little for movement among local communities. Its design reveals economic priorities, but the benefits and burdens still need to be traced across groups. Commodity specialisation could expose producers to distant price changes. Migration also ranged across different constraints: indentured contracts, forced displacement and wage migration cannot be treated as one identical process. A signed contract does not by itself establish equal bargaining power or accurate recruitment information. Examine recruitment, work conditions, legal restrictions and possibilities of return.

workedExamples.prompt: Analyse a hypothetical railway running from mines to a port but bypassing nearby farming settlements.
steps: Its route directly serves extraction and export.
Farmers may receive few transport benefits if they lack stations or affordable access.
workedExamples.conclusion: The line can increase export capacity while distributing gains unevenly.

flashcards.back: Heavy reliance on a narrow range of products and their markets.

flashcards.front: Does infrastructure automatically serve all residents equally?
flashcards.back: No.
Labour bound by a contract for a specified term, often under restrictive conditions.

flashcards.front: Does a signature prove equal bargaining power?
flashcards.back: No.

modules.title: 1900 onward: Global wars and political crises
modules.focus: Distinguish structural pressures from decisions that escalate conflict.
explanation: Twentieth-century wars involved industrial production, imperial connections and mass mobilisation. Alliances and rivalries created pressures, while leaders’ decisions shaped escalation. A global account includes colonial troops, civilian labour and conflict beyond European battlefields.

Economic crises and political instability contributed to authoritarian movements in some states, but outcomes differed. Genocide involves intentional destruction of a protected group in whole or part; historical analysis examines ideology, institutions, decisions and the people targeted rather than treating mass violence as inevitable.

workedExample.prompt: Explain how an imperial conflict in Europe could involve communities elsewhere.
steps: Empires drew soldiers, labour, food and materials from colonial territories.
Wartime disruption and participation could also reshape political expectations in those territories.

misconception.claim: The world wars affected only states on the main battlefronts.
misconception.correction: Mobilisation, empire, trade disruption and displacement spread effects much more widely.

questions.prompt: Why is a chronology of events insufficient to explain a war?
questions.answer: It shows sequence but must be linked to causes, interests and decisions explaining why escalation occurred.

questions.prompt: What evidence could illuminate civilian wartime experience?
questions.answer: Diaries, ration records, displacement data and oral histories can reveal labour, scarcity and disruption.

questions.prompt: Why should colonial troops not be described only as instruments of European governments?
questions.hint: Consider their own experiences and aims.
hints: Consider their own experiences and aims.
questions.answer: They acted within unequal imperial systems. Individuals and communities had varied motives and constraints. Their experiences and later claims belong in the explanation.
checkpoints: They acted within unequal imperial systems.
Individuals and communities had varied motives and constraints.
Their experiences and later claims belong in the explanation.

questions.prompt: Explain why comparing two authoritarian regimes requires more than noting that both used repression.
questions.answer: Repression is a relevant similarity. Ideology, institutions and targeted groups can differ. A comparison should explain those differences rather than treating the regimes as interchangeable.
checkpoints: Ideology, institutions and targeted groups can differ.
A comparison should explain those differences rather than treating the regimes as interchangeable.

notes.title: 1900 onward: Global wars and political crises in depth
paragraphs: Global war connected fronts through empire, production and finance. Colonial soldiers and civilian workers contributed to conflicts whose political decisions were often made elsewhere, yet they also pursued their own claims and goals. Economic crisis could undermine confidence in governments, but responses differed across institutions and societies. Authoritarianism therefore requires a case-specific explanation. Mass violence likewise needs analysis of ideology, organisations and deliberate actions. Studying genocide through only aggregate death counts misses how groups were identified, persecuted and targeted, as well as the experiences and resistance of the people affected.

workedExamples.prompt: Explain how a hypothetical European power's war can alter a colony's economy.
steps: Military demand redirects local labour and supplies.
Recruitment and taxation transfer resources towards the war effort.
workedExamples.conclusion: The colony experiences the conflict even without a major battle on its territory.

flashcards.front: What makes a conflict global beyond battlefield location?
flashcards.back: Linked labour, resources, finance and imperial participation.

flashcards.front: Does crisis produce one inevitable political outcome?
flashcards.back: No.
They can reveal mobilisation and its social reach.
Experience and agency absent from many administrative records.

modules.title: Cold War rivalry and decolonisation
modules.focus: Analyse local actors alongside competing superpowers.
explanation: Cold War rivalry shaped alliances, aid, interventions and ideological competition. Local conflicts were not merely scripts written by superpowers: regional leaders and communities pursued their own goals while seeking or resisting external support.

Decolonisation followed varied paths involving negotiation, mass movements and armed struggle. Political independence did not necessarily remove economic dependence or internal divisions. Non-alignment offered some states a strategy for pursuing autonomy amid bloc pressure, with different practices and results.

workedExample.prompt: Explain why a newly independent state might accept aid without wanting permanent bloc alignment.
steps: Aid could support immediate development or security aims.
Leaders might seek room to bargain with multiple partners and preserve independent policy choices.

misconception.claim: Every decolonising movement followed the same peaceful or violent path.
misconception.correction: Methods and outcomes depended on colonial policy, local organisation and wider circumstances.

questions.prompt: Why examine a local movement’s aims in a Cold War conflict?
questions.hint: Avoid reducing local actors to proxies.
questions.answer: Their land, national or social goals may explain choices that superpower rivalry alone cannot.

questions.prompt: How could economic dependence persist after independence?
questions.answer: Reliance on a narrow export base, foreign investment or external credit could limit policy options despite formal sovereignty.

questions.prompt: Why should a local civil conflict during the Cold War not be explained only through superpower rivalry?
questions.answer: Local political and social conflicts have their own histories. External support can alter their course. A full account explains how local aims and international rivalry interact.
checkpoints: Local political and social conflicts have their own histories.
External support can alter their course.
A full account explains how local aims and international rivalry interact.

questions.prompt: A state gains independence but relies on one export commodity. Explain one continuing constraint.
hints: Distinguish formal rule from economic structure.
questions.answer: Political authority has changed. Revenue remains exposed to the commodity's external market. Economic dependence can persist without direct colonial government.
checkpoints: Revenue remains exposed to the commodity's external market.
Economic dependence can persist without direct colonial government.

notes.title: Cold War rivalry and decolonisation in depth
paragraphs: Decolonisation changed formal sovereignty through varied combinations of negotiation, mass organisation and armed struggle. Independence did not settle every boundary, economic relationship or internal conflict. Cold War powers offered aid and intervention, while local leaders sought room to pursue their own priorities. The 1955 Bandung Conference brought Asian and African governments together around issues including decolonisation and development. Non-alignment should be understood as an effort to preserve autonomy, not a claim that every participating state was equally distant from both blocs at every moment. Policy and practice require separate examination.

workedExamples.prompt: Assess a hypothetical newly independent state accepting a foreign-built dam while refusing a permanent military base.
steps: The dam serves an economic development aim.
Rejecting the base limits a deeper strategic commitment.
workedExamples.conclusion: Accepting aid need not mean accepting every donor demand, although financial dependence may still constrain choices.

flashcards.back: Authority to govern a political community without an external ruler.
Decolonisation, development and international relations.

flashcards.front: Does non-alignment mean no foreign relationships?
flashcards.back: No.

flashcards.front: Did independence remove all economic dependence?
flashcards.back: No.

modules.title: Global connections and unequal consequences
explanation: Late twentieth-century and later globalisation accelerated flows of goods, finance, information and people. Transport and communication technologies reduced some barriers, while states and institutions still shaped access. Greater connection does not mean that every place has equal influence.

Global challenges such as environmental damage and disease transmission cross borders, encouraging cooperation and conflict over responsibility. Compare the scale of a problem with the institutions able to respond, and identify who benefits or bears costs in a proposed solution.

workedExample.prompt: A product is designed, assembled and sold in different countries. Explain one consequence.
steps: Production links workers and firms across several economies.
A disruption in one location can affect supply elsewhere, revealing both efficiency gains and shared vulnerability.

misconception.correction: States still influence borders, regulation, investment and the distribution of benefits.

questions.prompt: Why can cheaper digital communication increase both opportunity and inequality?
questions.answer: It expands potential reach, but differences in connectivity, skills and control of platforms shape who can benefit.

questions.prompt: Why does an environmental problem crossing borders create a coordination challenge?
questions.hint: Consider separate authorities and shared effects.
questions.answer: Actions in one state can impose costs elsewhere, while governments differ over responsibility, incentives and enforcement.

questions.prompt: Why might a transport disruption in one port affect factories in another country?
questions.answer: Factories may rely on components passing through that port. Delay interrupts the supply sequence. Cross-border dependence transmits the disruption beyond its starting location.
checkpoints: Factories may rely on components passing through that port.
Cross-border dependence transmits the disruption beyond its starting location.

questions.prompt: Explain one reason a global environmental agreement can face disagreement over responsibility.
questions.answer: States may have contributed differently to the problem. Their resources for responding differ. Groups bearing the greatest harm may not be those controlling the most emissions or decisions.
checkpoints: States may have contributed differently to the problem.
Groups bearing the greatest harm may not be those controlling the most emissions or decisions.

notes.title: Global connections and unequal consequences in depth
paragraphs: Globalisation joins production, finance and communication across borders, but states and firms still decide how those connections are organised. Standardised transport and faster information can reduce some transaction costs while concentrating advantages in well-connected places. A global production chain distributes tasks, risks and value unevenly; assembly location alone does not identify who captures the largest share. Environmental effects also cross borders while regulations remain divided among jurisdictions. Analyse the scale of the problem, the actors controlling decisions and the groups bearing costs. Greater connection does not automatically produce equal bargaining power.

workedExamples.prompt: Trace a hypothetical phone designed in country A, assembled in B and sold in C.
steps: Different locations contribute design, labour, components, logistics and retail.
The selling price is divided among these activities and firms; assembly wages are only one part.
workedExamples.conclusion: The chain demonstrates interdependence without establishing that each location receives equal value.

flashcards.back: Linked stages that create and distribute a product.

flashcards.front: Does assembly location show all value captured?
flashcards.back: No.

flashcards.front: Why do cross-border problems challenge regulation?
flashcards.back: Effects and legal jurisdictions may not align.
No.
